pharm: Prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractory period mainly by blocking potassium channels, with additional sodium- and calcium-channel and non-competitive alpha/beta-adrenergic blocking actions
quick: Oral load 800-1600 mg/day until response, then 400 mg/day maintenance; IV 150 mg then 1 mg/min
Take consistently with respect to food; food increases absorption
Can cause fetal harm (thyroid/neurodevelopment); use only if essential
Excreted in milk in significant amounts; breastfeeding not recommended
No specific dose adjustment; not significantly renally cleared
Hepatotoxic - monitor LFTs; reduce/discontinue if enzymes rise
ECG/QT, thyroid, LFTs, chest X-ray/PFTs, eyes, electrolytes
summary: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic for documented, life-threatening recurrent ventricular fibrillation and haemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia unresponsive to or intolerant of other agents. Oral therapy uses a loading dose of 800-1600 mg/day until response (usually 1-3 weeks), reduced to 600-800 mg/day for a month and then a maintenance dose of usually 400 mg/day; IV loading is 150 mg followed by 1 mg/min then 0.5 mg/min. It carries a BOXED WARNING for potentially fatal pulmonary toxicity (interstitial/alveolar pneumonitis), hepatotoxicity, and proarrhythmia (worsening of arrhythmia). Because of substantial toxicity it is reserved for life-threatening arrhythmias and requires baseline and periodic chest X-ray, pulmonary, thyroid, liver and eye monitoring.
indications: Documented, life-threatening recurrent haemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia in patients refractory to or intolerant of other antiarrhythmics

dosage.d: 800 to 1600 mg/day until initial therapeutic response (usually 1-3 weeks)
dosage.n: Correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia and obtain baseline tests first

dosage.d: Usually 400 mg/day (range 200-600 mg/day); use lowest effective dose
dosage.n: Lowest effective dose to limit toxicity

dosage.d: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min; supplemental 150 mg over 10 min for breakthrough VF/VT
dosage.t: Continuous infusion (about 1 mg/min average over 24 h)
dosage.n: Use an in-line filter; central line preferred for concentrations >2 mg/mL

admin: Obtain baseline chest X-ray, pulmonary-function tests, thyroid-function tests and liver aminotransferases before starting; correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia
Take oral doses consistently with regard to meals (food increases and standardises absorption)
Initiate or change therapy in a setting with continuous ECG monitoring because of proarrhythmia risk
For IV use, prefer a central venous catheter, use an in-line filter, and avoid prolonged infusion through PVC tubing/DEHP where possible
Use the lowest effective maintenance dose to minimise cumulative toxicity
Counsel on sun protection (photosensitivity) and the long half-life (effects persist for weeks after stopping)
moa: Amiodarone is predominantly a class III antiarrhythmic: it blocks myocardial potassium channels, prolonging the action-potential duration and effective refractory period in atrial and ventricular tissue and increasing the QT interval. It also blocks inactivated sodium channels (class I action), has calcium-channel-blocking (class IV) effects, and exerts non-competitive alpha- and beta-adrenergic antagonism (class II action). These combined effects slow conduction, reduce automaticity and AV/sinus node function, and suppress re-entrant arrhythmias. It is highly lipophilic with extensive tissue accumulation and a very long half-life.

absolute: Severe sinus-node dysfunction with marked sinus bradycardia
Second- or third-degree AV block, or bradycardia causing syncope, without a functioning pacemaker
Known hypersensitivity to amiodarone or iodine
relative: Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or drugs causing torsades de pointes
monitor: ECG and QT interval; heart rate/rhythm
Pulmonary symptoms; periodic chest X-ray and PFTs
Serum electrolytes and levels of interacting drugs (digoxin, warfarin)

preg: Amiodarone and its iodine content cross the placenta and can cause fetal harm, including neonatal hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, goitre, bradycardia and adverse neurodevelopmental effects. Use during pregnancy only when there is no safer alternative for a life-threatening maternal arrhythmia.
lact: Amiodarone and its active metabolite are excreted into breast milk in significant amounts and the iodine load poses a risk to the infant's thyroid. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: Amiodarone is not significantly eliminated by the kidneys, so no specific dose adjustment is required in renal impairment; monitoring for systemic toxicities still applies.
hepatic: Amiodarone can cause hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fatal hepatic failure. Obtain baseline and periodic liver enzymes; reduce the dose or discontinue if levels exceed three times normal or double from an elevated baseline, or if clinical liver injury occurs.

major: Warfarin - amiodarone potentiates anticoagulation; reduce warfarin dose and monitor INR closely
Digoxin - increases digoxin levels; halve the digoxin dose and monitor
Other QT-prolonging/antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g. sotalol, class I agents, fluoroquinolones, some antipsychotics) - additive QT prolongation and torsades risk
Simvastatin/lovastatin - increased myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk (limit statin dose)
moderate: Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers - additive bradycardia, AV block and hypotension
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. grapefruit juice, protease inhibitors) - increase amiodarone levels
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin) - reduce amiodarone levels; amiodarone also raises phenytoin levels
Cyclosporine, dabigatran and other substrates of P-gp/CYP - increased exposure
minor: May increase levels of various CYP2C9/3A4 substrates
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice raises amiodarone levels and should be avoided; take consistently with regard to meals
interactions.diagnostics: Causes ECG QT prolongation; alters thyroid-function test results; monitor LFTs, TSH/free T4, INR and digoxin levels

common: Bradycardia, fatigue, tremor, ataxia, sleep disturbance
serious: Pulmonary toxicity - interstitial/alveolar pneumonitis, pulmonary fibrosis (can be fatal)
Proarrhythmia - worsening arrhythmia, torsades de pointes, marked bradycardia/heart block
Severe thyroid dysfunction (thyroid storm or myxoedema)
Optic neuropathy/neuritis with potential vision loss
rare: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS
emergency: Torsades de pointes or symptomatic bradyarrhythmia

monitoring: Baseline and periodic ECG (QT interval, rate, rhythm)
Chest X-ray and pulmonary-function tests at baseline and periodically (every 3-6 months)
Liver aminotransferases at baseline and periodically
Thyroid-function tests (TSH, free T4) at baseline and every 6 months
Ophthalmologic assessment for visual symptoms or corneal/optic changes
Serum electrolytes, and INR/digoxin levels when co-prescribed
counsel: This medicine treats a serious heart-rhythm problem and needs regular blood, lung, thyroid and eye checks
Protect your skin from the sun and use sunscreen; your skin may take on a grey-blue tint over time
Report new cough or breathlessness, yellowing of the skin/eyes, vision changes or marked tiredness promptly
It interacts with many drugs - tell every prescriber you take it; do not start new medicines or grapefruit juice without checking
The drug stays in the body for weeks after stopping, so side effects and interactions can persist
Do not stop or change the dose without medical advice
pk: Oral antiarrhythmic effect delayed (days to weeks even with loading); IV onset within hours
Oral plasma Tmax approximately 3-7 hours; full tissue loading takes weeks
Very long and variable; terminal elimination half-life averages ~58 days (range ~15-142 days)
Effects and drug interactions persist for weeks to months after discontinuation
Store tablets at controlled room temperature, protect from light and moisture; protect IV solution from light
pearls: BOXED WARNING: potentially fatal pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity and proarrhythmia - reserve for life-threatening arrhythmias
Extremely long half-life (~58 days) - loading needed, and effects/interactions persist long after stopping
Major interactions: reduce warfarin and halve digoxin; avoid additive QT-prolonging drugs
Baseline and periodic chest X-ray/PFTs, LFTs, thyroid tests and eye review are mandatory
Causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism via its iodine load; correct electrolytes before starting
Counsel on photosensitivity and the characteristic slate-grey skin discoloration
missed: If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time - do not take a double dose. Because amiodarone has a very long half-life, one missed dose has little immediate effect, but tell your doctor if you miss several.
overdose: Overdose may cause bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, QT prolongation with torsades, and hepatotoxicity. There is no specific antidote and amiodarone is not dialysable. Manage supportively: monitor ECG and blood pressure, treat bradycardia with a beta-agonist or temporary pacing, and treat hypotension with inotropes/fluids; magnesium and overdrive pacing for torsades.
